purpose: Lamotrigine is used to help control seizures in people with epilepsy. It is also used to help stabilize mood in adults with bipolar disorder, especially to help prevent the low (depressive) episodes. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_it_works: Your brain sends electrical signals between nerve cells, and sometimes those signals can become overactive or unbalanced. Lamotrigine works by calming those overactive signals, kind of like a dimmer switch that turns down the electrical activity in your brain. This helps prevent seizures and keeps your mood more stable.
common_side_effects: Some people notice dizziness, headache, blurred or double vision, or feeling unsteady or clumsy. You might also feel tired, have an upset stomach, or notice a mild skin rash. Most of these tend to improve as your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: A serious skin rash can develop, especially in children or if the dose is increased too quickly — contact your doctor right away if you notice any rash. In rare cases, the rash can be life-threatening. Lamotrigine may also cause mood changes or suicidal thoughts — let your doctor or a trusted person know right away if you feel worse emotionally. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can trigger seizures.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very individual and your doctor will start you on a low dose and increase it slowly over several weeks to reduce the risk of side effects and rash. A common starting dose for adults is 25 mg once daily, gradually increasing over weeks to a typical maintenance dose of 100 to 400 mg per day, depending on what you are being treated for and other medications you take. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
